events.title: ESL Classes with Evergreen Valley College (EVC) - ESL 501: Reading & Writing 1

cases.refreshed: Develop your English language skills by practicing speaking, listening, reading, writing, vocabulary, pronunciation, and grammar. Do you want to build your English language skills and your confidence? This beginning non-credit ESL course is free! ESL 501 Reading & Writing 1. What will you learn in this class? This is a non-credit, high-beginning-level integrated ESL skills course emphasizing basic reading, writing, grammar, and vocabulary. Students will learn to comprehend frequently used words in context, use learned phrases and sentences to express ideas in basic writing, understand basic grammar structures, and read simplified material. Course Information: Starts: August 25, 2026; Ends: December 10, 2026; Meeting Days: Tuesday, Wednesday, and Thursday; Time: 10:30 AM - 12:30 PM; Instructor: Michelle N. Henninger. Before the classes start, you must complete a Guided Self-Placement (GSP). This is not a test—it's simply an assessment to help us place you in the most appropriate ESL class based on your current English level. We will assist you with the application and registration process in person at the Edenvale Branch Library. Space is limited.

events.title: Non-Fiction Book Discussion – Finders Keepers: a Tale of Archaeological Plunder and Obsession

cases.refreshed: In December the Cupertino Library Non-Fiction book discussion will talk about Finders Keepers: a Tale of Archaeological Plunder and Obsession by Craig Childs. (2010) Journalist Craig Childs documents his efforts to find and preserve precious and ancient artifacts from the American Southwest. Artifacts that could hold the keys to answering questions about the people who made and used them. From lonely archeological digs in the deserts of Arizona and New Mexico, to high end art galleries and museums in New York and Boston, Childs had to not only protect the artifacts themselves, but to also himself from ruthless art smugglers, risking his life and freedom multiple times. Childs' book also brings up the difficult questions about who the past, and its archaeological finds truly belong to. An archaeologist may be praised for excavating an ancient site and sharing their finds with a famous museum. But someone who steals a precious relic from a museum collection because they believe it is sacred and rightfully belongs back where it was found is called a thief, which one of them is actually in the wrong? The Non-fiction Book Discussion group meets on the second Sunday of each month at 11 am. All meetings are held in Room 201B. Sponsored by The Friends of the Cupertino Library. For accessibility accommodations (e.g., ASL), please fill out the online form at sccld.org/accessibility 7+ days prior to the event. If you need assistance with the form, speak with a staff member at your local library, call (408) 540-3945, or email us at ask@sccl.org.
